In the morning she had been found dead in bed, apparently without having suffered. Sir Mathew Reid was called immediately, but of course he could do nothing. Her funeral would take place on the 22nd at Beauchamp Chalcote. A few days before her death, she had written a will leaving Lord Arthur her small house in Curzon Street, together with its furniture, her personal belongings, and her pictures. The exceptions were her collection of miniature paintings, which would go to her sister, Lady Margaret Rufford, and her amethyst necklace, which she left to Sybil Merton. The inheritance was not worth a great deal. Still, Mr. Mansfield, the lawyer, was very anxious for Lord Arthur to return immediately if he could. There were many bills to settle, and Lady Clementina had never kept proper accounts.

Lord Arthur was deeply moved by Lady Clementina’s kindness in remembering him, and felt that Mr. Podgers had much to answer for. Yet his love for Sybil was stronger than every other feeling. Knowing that he had done his duty brought him comfort and peace. By the time he reached Charing Cross, he felt entirely happy.

The Mertons welcomed him warmly. Sybil made him promise never to let anything separate them again, and they set the wedding for June 7th. Life seemed bright and beautiful once more, and all his former happiness returned.

One day, however, he was sorting through the house in Curzon Street with Lady Clementina’s lawyer and Sybil. As they burned bundles of faded letters and emptied drawers of assorted rubbish, the young woman suddenly gave a small, delighted cry.

“What have you found, Sybil?” Lord Arthur asked, looking up from his work with a smile.

“This lovely little silver sweet box, Arthur. Isn’t it charming and Dutch? Please let me have it! I know amethysts won’t suit me until I’m over eighty.”

It was the box that had contained the aconitine.

Lord Arthur gave a start, and his cheeks coloured faintly. He had almost completely forgotten his action. It seemed a strange coincidence that Sybil, for whose sake he had endured all that terrible worry, should be the first to remind him of it.

“Of course you may have it, Sybil. I gave it to poor Lady Clem myself.”

“Oh, thank you, Arthur! And may I have the sweet as well? I never imagined Lady Clementina liked sweets. I thought she was much too intellectual.”

Lord Arthur turned deathly pale as a horrible thought entered his mind.

Throughout his present brief visit, Emma had seen scarcely anything of him, though enough to feel that the first encounter was behind her, and to conclude that the blend of resentment and self-importance now marking his manner was no improvement. Indeed, she was beginning to marvel that she had ever found him agreeable. The sight of him was bound so closely to unpleasant sensations that, save as a moral exercise—a penance, a lesson, a salutary humiliation of her pride—she would gladly have learned that she need never see him again. She wished him every happiness; but he caused her pain, and his prosperity at twenty miles’ distance would have pleased her best.

His marriage, however, must surely soften the discomfort of his continuing to live in Highbury. It would forestall many needless anxieties and ease many awkward situations. A Mrs. Elton would justify any alteration in their intercourse; their old familiarity could diminish unnoticed. Their civil relations would almost begin afresh.

Emma gave little thought to the lady herself. Doubtless she was sufficiently good for Mr. Elton, sufficiently accomplished for Highbury, sufficiently handsome—probably to appear plain beside Harriet. Concerning her connections Emma felt entirely secure, convinced that, after boasting of his own claims and scorning Harriet’s, he had gained nothing. On this subject the truth seemed discoverable. What sort of person she was remained uncertain, but who she was could be established; and apart from the ten thousand pounds, she seemed in no respect Harriet’s superior. She contributed neither a distinguished name nor ancestry nor alliance. Miss Hawkins was the younger of two daughters of a Bristol—merchant, as of course one must call him. Yet the whole proceeds of his commercial career appeared so modest that one might fairly suppose the dignity of his trade equally modest. She had customarily spent part of each winter in Bath, but Bristol was her home, the very centre of Bristol. Although her parents had died some years earlier, an uncle survived—in the law. No more precisely honourable description had been ventured than that he was in the law, and the daughter had lived with him. Emma imagined him some attorney’s overworked subordinate, too dull to advance. The entire magnificence of the connection seemed to rest upon the elder sister, who had married very well indeed: a gentleman living in great style near Bristol, who maintained two carriages! There the account concluded; there lay Miss Hawkins’ glory.

“Absolutely delightful!” cried Mrs. Clay, though she did not dare look toward Anne. “Just like a father and son! Dear Miss Elliot, surely I may say father and son?”

“Oh, I don’t forbid anyone to use any words. If you insist on having such ideas! But honestly, I hardly notice that he pays me more attention than other men do.”

“My dear Miss Elliot!” exclaimed Mrs. Clay. She raised her hands and eyes, then conveniently expressed the rest of her amazement by saying nothing.

“Well, my dear Penelope, you needn’t be so anxious about him. I did invite him, you know. He went away smiling. Once I learned that he really was spending all of tomorrow with his friends at Thornberry Park, I took pity on him.”

Anne admired her friend’s skill at pretending. Mrs. Clay managed to show equal pleasure while expecting Mr. Elliot and when he actually arrived, although his presence must interfere with her chief aim. She could hardly help hating the sight of him. Yet she put on a helpful, peaceful expression and appeared perfectly content to have only half as much opportunity to attend to Sir Walter as she otherwise would.

Anne herself was deeply distressed when Mr. Elliot entered the room, and it hurt her to have him come over and speak to her. Before this, she had felt that he could not always be entirely sincere. Now everything about him seemed false. His respectful attention to her father was disgusting when compared with the way he had spoken about him in the past. Remembering his cruelty to Mrs. Smith, Anne could barely endure his current smiles and gentle manner, or listen to his false expressions of fine feelings.

She intended to avoid changing her behaviour so obviously that he would protest. Above all, she wanted to prevent questions or a public scene. Still, she planned to treat him as coolly as their family connection allowed, and to withdraw as quietly as possible from the unnecessary closeness into which she had gradually been drawn. She was therefore more careful and distant than she had been the night before.

He tried to make her curious again about where and how he had previously heard her praised. He badly wanted the satisfaction of having her press him for more information. But the spell had ended. He discovered that the warmth and excitement of a public gathering were needed to awaken his modest cousin’s vanity—or, at least, he discovered that he could not awaken it now. None of the attempts he dared make, among the insistent demands of the others, had any effect.
